text:
The Volvo station wagon belonged to the Hawthorne Foundation, bequeathed by a trustee’s widow in the nineties under the impression that artists required heavy Swedish steel to transport their epiphanies. It smelled of damp dog, old menthols, and rotting pine needles. When Arthur turned the key, the engine cleared its throat with a phlegmy, metallic reluctance.

"She’s a grand dame," Clara said from the passenger seat. Her bare feet were propped on the cracked vinyl dashboard, toenails painted a chipped aubergine she had applied during her second week at the colony, right before abandoning her sonnet cycle about the siege of Leningrad.

"She’s a liability," Arthur said, coaxing the gearshift into reverse. The transmission gave a dull clunk. "If the alternator dies on Route 9, we’ll have to barter your stipend for a tow."

"They only gave us half up front," Clara reminded him, sliding tortoiseshell sunglasses down her nose. "And I spent mine on gin and those tins of Portuguese sardines you like. We’d have to leave them you. You look like you could split cordwood for a taciturn Maine mechanic."

Arthur did not look like he could split cordwood. He was a thirty-four-year-old adjunct professor of architectural history from Chicago with pale calves and spectacles that left permanent indentations on his nose. Yet for twenty-seven days at the Hawthorne Colony, he had passed himself off as a man of brooding physicality—largely due to a lost-and-found fisherman’s sweater and the fact that Clara, who lived in Brooklyn, had a wildly recalibrated sense of the rugged.

It was the twenty-eighth day. Tomorrow, local taxis would disperse the twelve fellows back to their respective anxieties. Arthur was returning to a Hyde Park sublet and a half-finished monograph on municipal bathhouses; Clara was returning to a fourth-floor walk-up she shared with a man named Julian, whom she referred to in week one as "my partner," in week two as "Julian," and by week three—shortly after she and Arthur began meeting in the unheated fern conservatory—simply as "the person who waters my ficus."

"You’re going to miss the bridge," she said, looking at a crumpled geological map.

"I missed it three miles ago," Arthur said, watching the September light catch the small scar beneath her ear. "We’re taking the scenic detour."

"Good. I’m not ready for the ocean. It’s very final. Just sitting there, waiting for us to have a moment of profound reckoning." She tossed the map into the backseat atop a canvas tote containing two threadbare towels, a bottle of dry Riesling wrapped in Arthur’s extra sweater, and a hard green pear.

They had not slept together—not in the prosecutorial sense. Theirs was a romance of proximity and curfews, conducted in the margins of the colony’s monastic schedule. It consisted of knees pressed together beneath the refectory table; shared cigarettes behind the compost heaps; and three breathless hours in Arthur’s converted icehouse studio, where they had stripped to their waists and kissed until their mouths were bruised, stopping only because the floorboards creaked with such theatrical violence it felt as though the ghost of Mrs. Hawthorne were taking notes. 

There was an unspoken consensus that consummation would ruin its lines. An architectural folly was charming precisely because you couldn't live in it; install plumbing, and it became merely a small, damp house.

By the time they reached Popham Beach, the afternoon had curdled into the pewter-colored melancholy of a New England autumn. Arthur parked in a sandy lot bordered by hissing dune grass. The kiosk was boarded up, a sign reading *SEE YOU IN MAY* nailed across the window.

"We’re trespassing against the season," Clara said, stepping out. The wind whipped her dark hair across her mouth. She wore Arthur’s corduroy jacket over a thin cotton sundress inappropriate for fifty-two degrees.

"Put the sweater on," Arthur said, reaching into the back. 

She allowed him to pull the heavy wool over her head. For a second she was trapped inside the weave, and Arthur steadied her by the hips. Through the thin cotton, her hipbones felt startlingly sharp, temporary, like the frame of a kite. When her head emerged, her hair stood up in static-charged aureoles. She touched his cheek with cold fingers. "You have a pine needle. You’re turning into the car, Arthur."

"It’s a slow process," he said. "First the upholstery, then the chassis."

They walked onto the hard-packed expanse of the low-tide beach, where the river met the Atlantic in a choppy confluence. A quarter-mile out, a granite island sat like a clenched fist, topped with a ruined fort. 

"Can we walk out to it?" Clara asked.

"Low tide was at two-thirty," Arthur said, checking his grandfather's Timex. "It’s almost four. We’d have to swim back."

"What a scandal for the newsletter," she murmured, linking her arm through his. "Think of the memorial fellowships. The Arthur Pendelton Grant for Indecisive Historians. The Clara Vance Prize for Women Who Can't Finish a Fourteen-Line Poem."

"You finished six."

"Five and a half. The last one has no volta. It just complains about the cabbage soup and stops." She kicked a dried horseshoe crab shell. "Julian thinks I’m coming back with a chapbook. His friend in Red Hook has a Risograph machine. They’re going to bind it with butcher’s twine."

The name hung in the salt air, dense and unhelpful. 

"Tell him you burned them," Arthur said tightly. "In a fit of Gogolian despair."

"Julian doesn't like romance," she said simply. "He likes projects. I’m a project. He’s currently fermenting hot sauce in the linen closet. It smells like vinegar and old pennies."

She crouched beside a tide pool, poking a finger into a green anemone. Arthur stood over her, feeling a useless surge of resentment. He resented the Risograph; he resented that in twenty-four hours she would be on an Amtrak train, recalibrating her vocabulary for a life in which he was merely an anecdote.

"Come to Chicago," he said. The words simply dislodged themselves from his teeth.

Clara kept her finger in the freezing water. "When?"

"Tomorrow," Arthur said, feeling a reckless urge to furnish the absurdity. "Change your ticket. We’ll take the Lake Shore Limited from Boston. Twenty-two hours. We can eat microwaved cheeseburgers in the lounge car and look at Syracuse in the dark."

Clara slowly stood, wiping her finger on his sweater, and looked toward the island. The sandbar was disappearing, the slate-colored water chewing away at the wet earth.

"Arthur," she said, using the tone she used when a metaphor failed. "You have a nineteen-year-old grader who emails you four times a day about his digestion. Your apartment has a view of an airshaft."

"It’s a very wide airshaft," he tried to smile. 

"And what would I do there while you teach sophomores why the Pantheon didn't fall down?" She turned to him, eyes dark and wind-stung. "In Brooklyn, I have a life I spent six years building out of cheap plywood. It’s drafty, and the person I built it with irritates me in ways that have become structural, like a warped floorboard you just step over. If I go with you tomorrow, by Tuesday we’ll be looking at each other over takeout Pad Thai, wondering why neither of us sounds as clever as we did when someone else was cooking our dinner in a nineteenth-century farmhouse."

She was right. The residency was a biosphere, stripped of utility bills and bad credit. In Maine, he was a man who carried wine in a wool sweater; in Chicago, he bought late-night rotisserie chickens at Jewel-Osco and worried about tenure.

They retreated to a hollow in the dunes sheltered by scrubby Rosa rugosa bushes. Arthur used his pocketknife to uncork the Riesling, crumbling the bottom third of the cork into the pale gold liquid.

"Extra fiber," Clara said, taking a long drink before spitting a fleck of cork onto her chin.

Arthur brushed it away with his thumb, letting his palm come to rest against her warm neck. She leaned into his hand, closing her eyes. "I’m going to miss your hands. Julian has very small hands. Like a colonial doll’s."

"That’s a terrible thing to say."

"I’m a terrible person. That’s why I’m a poet." She opened her eyes and passed the bottle. "What will you tell your colleagues about this place?"

Arthur drank; it tasted of green apples and disintegrated oak. "That the library had a complete run of *The Architectural Review* from the twenties. That the food was heavy on root vegetables."

"Will you tell them about me?"

"No," he said honestly.

Clara smiled crookedly. "Good. I don't want to be departmental gossip. I’ll tell Julian an architect bled my studio radiator. Which is true."

"I ruined my good handkerchief doing it."

"Frame it," she said. "Call it *Untitled (Iron Oxide on Cotton, 2023)*."

She leaned across the towel and kissed him. It wasn't frantic like the icehouse; it was slow, cold, and tasted of an ending. Arthur pulled her into his lap, his hand tangling in the coarse wool of his sweater, finding the shape of her ribs. He felt a sharp grief—not just for Clara, whom he barely knew, whose middle name was Frances, whose childhood dog was Spot—but for the version of himself that existed when she looked at him. It was an old literary vanity, mourning the mirror more than the woman, yet with his face pressed into her rosemary-scented shoulder, the distinction felt academic.

"The tide," Clara murmured.

A tongue of grey foam had licked into their hollow, setting one of her leather sandals afloat in freezing brine. 

"Christ," Arthur said, scrambling to grab the sodden shoe. 

They gathered their things in clumsy haste as the first needle-thin drops of evening rain began to fall, smelling of iron and dead kelp. They climbed the bank back to the Volvo, their knees crusted with wet sand. 

Arthur got in and turned the key. Nothing happened. Only a dry *click*, followed by the faint hum of the broken dashboard clock. He turned it again. *Click.*

"Is she dead?" Clara asked, shivering now, pulling her wet knees to her chest.

"The battery," Arthur said, looking up at the roof, where the small plastic map light glowed with a faint, jaundiced warmth. "You left the light on."

"Oh," she said guiltily. "Well. It was dark because of the trees."

As the rain began to drum against the windshield, blurring the pines into a green-grey smear, Arthur felt a strange, buoyant relief. They were going to miss the final communal dinner—roast pork with orchard apples—and the awkward exchanging of email addresses no one would use after Christmas. 

"I have no service," Arthur said, looking at his dead phone. "There’s a bait shop two miles back. I’ll walk."

"You’ll get trench foot," Clara said, looking at his steaming suede shoes. "You’ll die of exposure, like a minor character in a Hardy novel."

"I’ll be forty minutes," he said, reaching for the handle.

"Wait." She caught his sleeve. "Just sit for five minutes. Until the rain slackens."

It wouldn't slacken; it was a frontal system from the Maritimes, vast and indifferent. Tomorrow, their taxis would have their wipers on high all the way to the interstate. 

Arthur settled back into the sagging seat. The windows were fogging from their breath and damp clothes, enclosing them in a pearl-grey blindness that erased the ocean and the road back. Clara leaned her head on his shoulder, taking his hand and placing it inside the pocket of the corduroy jacket, wrapping her fingers around his knuckles.

"Tell me about the bathhouses," she said, watching the opaque windshield. "Why did Chicago build them?"

"Because the tenements didn't have tubs," he said, his voice small in the muffled box of the car. "In the eighteen-nineties. The city thought if immigrant laborers were clean, they’d be less inclined toward anarchism. They built them of red brick with terra-cotta dolphins. You got a towel, a cube of lard soap, and twenty minutes."

"Did it stop the anarchism?"

"No," Arthur said, watching a drop of water trace an erratic path down the glass. "They just had cleaner anarchists."

Clara laughed softly against his collarbone, then went quiet. Above them, the little yellow dome light flickered once, dimmed to the color of an old bruise, and went out entirely, leaving them in the gathering dark with the sound of rain on steel and the rhythmic thrum of the tide coming in to cover the sandbar, erasing their footprints one by one.
